title: Splitting the problem in half
objectives: Solve a problem by dividing it, solving the halves and combining.

screens.title: Two halves, one answer
screens.prose: Four daily returns, in basis points: 7, 2, 9 and 4. A function finds the largest by splitting the list in half, finding the largest of each half the same way, and keeping the larger.

state.caption: One item is its own largest. The numbers on the lines are what each call returns.

screens.question: Fill in what each call returns.

hints.text: A one-item list returns its item. What does `[7, 2]` keep from 7 and 2?
This call compares the answers of `[7]` and `[2]`.
`[7, 2]` keeps 7, `[9, 4]` keeps 9, and the whole list keeps the larger of 7 and 9.

feedback.correct: Each call keeps the larger of its two halves' answers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work up from the single items, keeping the larger of each pair.

byKey.r2c1: The whole list compares 7 and 9, the answers of its two halves.

explain.text: The single items answer at once. Each pair keeps its larger item, 7 and 9. The top call keeps the larger of those, 9, without ever comparing 2 with 4 directly.

screens.title: Where to split
screens.question: Which two calls does `max_rec(xs, 0, 7)` make?

options.why: You started the right half at `mid`, so index 3 is in both halves. Look at `mid + 1`.
You ended the left half at `mid - 1`. The code passes `mid` itself to the left half.
You rounded `(0 + 7) / 2` up. `//` rounds down, so `mid` is 3.

hints.text: Work out `mid = (0 + 7) // 2` first.
The left call takes `lo` to `mid`; the right call starts one after `mid`.
`mid` is 3, so the halves are 0 to 3 and 4 to 7.

feedback.correct: `mid` is 3, so the halves are 0 to 3 and 4 to 7, with no overlap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute `mid`, then read the two calls in the code.

byKey.overlap: You put index 3 in both halves. The right half starts at `mid + 1`.

explain.text: `(0 + 7) // 2` is 3, so the left half is indices 0 to 3 and the right half 4 to 7. Every index is in exactly one half, and both halves are smaller than the whole.

screens.title: How many calls
screens.prose: Here is every call `max_rec` makes on 8 numbers. A call on one index, where `lo == hi`, is the base case.
screens.question: How many calls does `max_rec(xs, 0, 7)` make in all, counting itself?

hints.text: Count the calls level by level.
The bottom level has one call per number.
Levels hold 1, 2, 4 and 8 calls: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the calls on every level, including the top.

byKey.leaves: You counted only the base cases. The calls above them count too.
byKey.inner: You counted only the calls that split. The 8 single-index calls count too.
byKey.levels: That is the number of levels. Count the calls on each level and add.
byKey.sixteen: The top level has one call, not two: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8$.

explain.text: The levels hold 1, 2, 4 and 8 calls, so 15 in all. In general $n$ numbers give $n$ base cases and $n - 1$ splits: $2n - 1$ calls. A single number, $n = 1$, is one call that answers at once.

screens.title: Pairs out of order
screens.prose: An **inversion** is a pair where the earlier number is bigger. `[3, 1, 4, 2]` splits into `[3, 1]` and `[4, 2]`, each with one inversion. The numbers on the lines are each half's count.
screens.question: How many inversions does `[3, 1, 4, 2]` have in all?

hints.text: The halves found (3, 1) and (4, 2). Which pairs span both halves?
Compare each number on the left with each on the right.
Across the halves only (3, 2) is out of order. Add it to the 2 inside the halves.

feedback.correct: 1 + 1 inside the halves, plus 1 pair across them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count inside each half, then across the split.

byKey.no-cross: You added the two halves and stopped. The combine step must count pairs across the split: (3, 2).
byKey.all-pairs: That is every pair. Count only those where the earlier number is bigger.
byKey.cross-only: That is the cross pair alone. Add the inversions inside each half.

explain.text: The halves give $1 + 1$. The combine step checks pairs across the split: 3 against 4 and 2, then 1 against 4 and 2. Only (3, 2) is out of order, so the total is 3.

screens.title: Keeping only one half
screens.prose: Binary search on sorted prices also splits in half. It looks at the middle price, then searches **one** half only. Each call halves the range.
screens.question: Starting from 1,024 sorted prices, how many calls until the range holds one price?

hints.text: 8 prices took 4 calls: 8, 4, 2, 1. Halve 1,024 the same way.
How many halvings take 1,024 down to 1?
$1024 = 2^{10}$, so 10 halvings. With the first call that makes 11 calls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the range sizes from 1,024 down to 1.

byKey.log: Ten is the number of halvings. Count the calls: one per range size, 1,024 down to 1.
byKey.half: One call per price in a half is far too many. Each call halves the range again.

explain.text: The sizes run 1,024, 512, 256, and so on down to 1: eleven sizes, one call each. That is $\log_2 1024 + 1$. We build binary search properly in a later lesson.

screens.title: Max by halves, power by squaring
screens.prose: Fast power halves $n$: $x^n = (x^{n/2})^2$ for even $n$, and $x \cdot (x^{(n-1)/2})^2$ for odd $n$. Return the value and the number of multiplications. An even step costs 1 (`h * h`), an odd step 2 (`h * h * x`). Base cases: $n = 0$ gives `(1, 0)`, $n = 1$ gives `(x, 0)`.
screens.question: Write `max_rec(xs, lo, hi)` by halves, as before, and `power_fast(x, n)` returning `(value, multiplications)`.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. Test 5 has 5,000 numbers; test 10 has $n = 10^9$, which one-at-a-time multiplying could never reach. Decimal answers pass when `math.isclose` agrees.

hints.text: `power_fast` calls itself once, on `n // 2`, then squares the result.
For odd $n$, `n // 2` drops a factor of $x$. Multiply it back in.
`h, m = power_fast(x, n // 2)`. Even: `return h * h, m + 1`. Odd: `return h * h * x, m + 2`.

feedback.correct: Both halve the problem, so their depth grows like $\log_2 n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 expects 100 on 5,000 numbers. A one-at-a-time recursion runs out of stack: split at `mid`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 expects `(243, 3)`. If you got 81, the odd case is missing its extra `* x`.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 expects `(1, 41)` for $n = 10^9$. Call `power_fast` once per level, on `n // 2`, and reuse the result.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. A `RecursionError` means a half did not shrink: check `mid + 1`.

explain.text: Halving means $n = 10^9$ needs only 30 levels and 41 multiplications, not a billion. The odd case adds one `* x`, because `n // 2` rounded down. Calling `power_fast` twice on `n // 2` instead of reusing `h` would undo the saving.

screens.title: A half that never shrinks
screens.question: What does `max_rec([5, 8], 0, 1)` do?

options.why: You expected both halves to shrink. With `mid` 0, the right half is 0 to 1: the same call again.
The left half does return 5, but the right call never finishes.
No index goes out of range. The same range repeats until the stack runs out.

hints.text: Work out `mid` for `lo = 0`, `hi = 1`.
This call has the same range as its parent.
`mid` is 0, so the right call is `max_rec(xs, 0, 1)` again, for ever.

feedback.correct: A half the same size as the whole never reaches the base case.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the two calls when `mid` is 0.

byKey.eight: You assumed the halves shrink. On two items the right half is the whole range again.
byKey.index: You expected a bad index. The ranges stay inside the list; they just never get smaller.

explain.text: With `lo = 0` and `hi = 1`, `mid` is 0. The right call gets 0 to 1, exactly the range it was given, so it repeats until `RecursionError`. Split as `lo..mid` and `mid + 1..hi`, and both halves are always smaller.

screens.title: Divide and conquer
screens.prose:
Every function here had three steps: **split** at `mid`, **solve** each half by the same function, **combine**.

$$x^n = \begin{cases} (x^{n/2})^2 & n \text{ even} \\ x \cdot (x^{(n-1)/2})^2 & n \text{ odd} \end{cases}$$

The halves must not overlap, and both must be smaller.
screens.question: How many calls does `max_rec` make on 16 numbers?

options.why: That counts only the base cases. The 15 calls that split count too.
That counts only the calls that split. Add the 16 base cases.
That is the number of levels: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 calls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the calls level by level: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

explain.text: The levels hold $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31$ calls. That is $2 \times 16 - 1$, the same pattern as 15 calls for 8 numbers.

screens.title: The odd case
screens.prose: We compute `power_fast(2, 5)` by hand. Each line says why it follows.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: `power_fast(2, 2)` needs `power_fast(2, 1)`, which returns 2: the base case
`power_fast(2, 2)` returns $2 \times 2 = 4$: 2 is even, so square the half
`power_fast(2, 5)` returns $4 \times 4 \times 2 = 32$: 5 is odd, so square, then one more 2

hints.text: Which call does the work first, the top one or the bottom one?
The calls go down to the base case, then the answers come back up.
Down: 5 needs 2, 2 needs 1. Up: 1 gives 2, then $2^2 = 4$, then $4^2 \times 2 = 32$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Calls go down first; answers come back up.

byKey.d4: The top call finishes last, so its line comes last.
byKey.d3: `power_fast(2, 2)` can square only after the base case has returned 2.

explain.text: Halving 5 gives 2 and drops a remainder of 1. Squaring $2^2$ gives only $2^4 = 16$, so the odd case multiplies by one more 2. Without that step the function returns 16, not 32.

screens.title: A year of daily growth
screens.prose: A strategy earns 0.02% a day. Over a year of 252 trading days, £1 grows to $1.0002^{252} \approx 1.0517$. You compute it with `power_fast`.

state.caption: The exponents `power_fast` visits. Lines show each call's cost.

screens.question: How many multiplications does `power_fast(1.0002, 252)` make?

hints.text: Each even step costs 1 multiplication; each odd step costs 2. The base case $n = 1$ costs 0.
Two of the steps are even. The rest above the base case are odd.
252 and 126 are even: 2. Then 63, 31, 15, 7 and 3 are odd: 10. Total 12.

feedback.correct: 12 multiplications, against 251 one at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 1 for each even exponent and 2 for each odd one above 1.

byKey.calls: 8 is the number of calls. Odd steps cost 2 multiplications each.
byKey.naive: 251 is the one-at-a-time count. Halving the exponent needs far fewer.
byKey.nobase1: You charged the call on 1 as an odd step. $n = 1$ is a base case: it returns $x$ for free.

explain.text: Two even steps cost 1 each and five odd steps cost 2 each: $2 + 10 = 12$. That is 7 squarings plus 5 extra factors of 1.0002, against 251 multiplications one day at a time. For a 10-year horizon of 2,520 days the halving needs only 16.

ideas: Divide and conquer: split the input at `mid`, solve each half with the same function, combine the two answers.
Split as `lo..mid` and `mid + 1..hi`, so the halves never overlap and both shrink. A half the same size as the whole recurses for ever.
Halving keeps the depth near $\log_2 n$: fast power reaches $x^{10^9}$ in 41 multiplications.

formula.name: Fast power
formula.tex: x^n = \begin{cases} (x^{n/2})^2 & n \text{ even} \\ x \cdot (x^{(n-1)/2})^2 & n \text{ odd} \end{cases}
formula.note: Compute the half once and reuse it; the odd case needs one extra factor of $x$.

summary.trap: Starting the right half at `mid` instead of `mid + 1`: on two items the half is the whole range, so the recursion never ends.

quiz.question: Merging a log of 3 trades with a log of 4, what is the most comparisons `a[0] <= b[0]` can make?

widget.accept: 6: one per trade placed before a log runs out

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each comparison places one trade. When does the comparing stop?

byKey.seven: The last trade is placed by a base case, when the other log is empty. No comparison is needed.
byKey.twelve: Each trade is compared only with the front of the other log, not with every trade in it.

explain.text: Each comparison places one trade and shortens one log. Once a log is empty, the base case returns the rest unchanged. So at most $3 + 4 - 1 = 6$ comparisons.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many additions turn 4 numbers into 1?
